author: NEWS10 ABC
title: Cambridge Central School District explores potential 'reorganization' - NewsBreak
text:
1 hours ago
CAMBRIDGE, N.Y. ( WTEN ) -- A northern Capital Region school district, which had to cut 21 positions after its budget failed twice earlier this year, is now looking into school district reorganization, and whether a potential merger could ease financial strains.
Cambridge CSD cuts 21 positions as contingency budget passes Roughly 25 community members showed up to the Cambridge Central School District auditorium to learn about reorganization, hearing from the district's lawyer, Erin Rose Morris.
Jessica Ziehm, who has two kids in the district, and also formerly served on the school board, said the presentation was productive.
Download our WTEN+ streaming app on Roku, Fire TV and Apple TV! "I think that was the biggest take home message for me tonight is, you know, the merger study that would have to be done," she said, "the agreeance between [two or more districts] to even think about starting to talk about this."
Get the latest news, weather, sports and entertainment delivered right to your inbox! The feasibility study Ziehm referenced is one of the first actions taken during the reorganization process, the timeline of which can take roughly a year.
One recent Capital Region example is the vote by the Troy City and Wynantskill Union Free School Districts in May to merge starting in the 2027-28 school year.
Wynantskill UFSD to dissolve in 2027, join Troy CSD One benefit of this process, according to Morris, is something in New York called Reorganization Incentive Building Aid, something the state budgeted roughly $3.6 million for. She said it's a good pathway to getting grants for improvements to school grounds.
"[It] allows us to upgrade and improve buildings, grounds and other school facilities because where school districts elect to merge, the state aid that comes in is actually quite generous," said Morris. "It gives us more resources, more programs, more support services and more opportunities."
Andrew Flynn, a lifelong community member with two kids in the district, saw the financial side of the pitch at the forefront.
"There's a fair bit of money in this merger stuff, it seems, from the state," he said. "It seems that they're really trying to incentivize districts getting together in different ways."
There are still details that would have to be worked out with whoever Cambridge eyes for a potential merger.
"Some of the rural districts, it may be harder," Flynn said. "We're so far apart that you may have kids on school busses for two, three hours accidentally."
This is step one for Cambridge. Ultimately, a decision like this is up to the community, and what they want for their students and teachers. A vote wouldn't be cast for at least another year if Cambridge and another school district were to decide to go through with a merger.
